hints: Focus on the classic test for halides with acidified silver nitrate, the colour and solubility of each silver halide is the key clue.
Remember that only silver chloride dissolves in dilute ammonia to give a colourless solution, silver bromide needs concentrated ammonia.
Notice the last step where adding acid brings the precipitate back, this confirms a reversible dissolving to form a complex ion that is destroyed by acid.
walkthrough:
**Recall the first test with acidified AgNO3**

All soluble halides give a precipitate of silver halide with $\text{Ag}^+(\text{aq})$ in the presence of $\text{HNO}_3(\text{aq})$. The nitric acid is just to remove other interfering ions like carbonate.

$$\text{Ag}^+(\text{aq}) + \text{X}^-(\text{aq}) \rightarrow \text{AgX}(\text{s})$$

**Use solubility in dilute ammonia to identify the halide**

This is the deciding test. $\text{AgCl}$ is white and dissolves in dilute $\text{NH}_3(\text{aq})$ to form the colourless complex ion. $\text{AgBr}$ is cream and only dissolves in concentrated $\text{NH}_3$. $\text{AgI}$ is yellow and is insoluble even in concentrated $\text{NH}_3$.

$$\text{AgCl}(\text{s}) + 2\text{NH}_3(\text{aq}) \rightarrow [\text{Ag}(\text{NH}_3)_2]^+(\text{aq}) + \text{Cl}^-(\text{aq})$$

**Explain the reappearance of precipitate with acid**

Adding excess $\text{HNO}_3$ reacts with the ammonia ligands in the complex, destroying it and freeing $\text{Ag}^+$ to re-precipitate with $\text{Cl}^-$. This confirms the precipitate dissolved reversibly, which only happens for chloride in dilute ammonia.

$$[\text{Ag}(\text{NH}_3)_2]^+(\text{aq}) + 2\text{H}^+(\text{aq}) + \text{Cl}^-(\text{aq}) \rightarrow \text{AgCl}(\text{s}) + 2\text{NH}_4^+(\text{aq})$$

**Conclude what J must be**

Only a chloride salt fits all three observations: precipitate, dissolve in dilute ammonia to a colourless solution, then re-precipitate on acidification. So J must contain $\text{Cl}^-$.

options.A: Correct. Sodium chloride provides $\text{Cl}^-$ which gives white $\text{AgCl}$ precipitate. $\text{AgCl}$ dissolves in dilute $\text{NH}_3$ to give colourless $[\text{Ag}(\text{NH}_3)_2]^+$ and $\text{Cl}^-$, then excess $\text{HNO}_3$ destroys the complex and re-precipitates white $\text{AgCl}$. This matches the scheme exactly.
options.B: Incorrect. Sodium bromide gives cream $\text{AgBr}$ precipitate, but $\text{AgBr}$ is insoluble in dilute $\text{NH}_3$ and only dissolves in concentrated $\text{NH}_3$. It would not give the colourless solution shown, so this is a common confusion between chloride and bromide solubility.
options.C: Incorrect. Potassium iodide gives yellow $\text{AgI}$ precipitate which is insoluble even in concentrated $\text{NH}_3$. It would stay as a precipitate and never form the colourless solution, so it fails at the second step.
options.D: Incorrect. Astatide is below iodide in Group 17, so silver astatide would be even less soluble than $\text{AgI}$. Like iodide, it would not dissolve in dilute $\text{NH}_3$ to give a colourless solution. Students choosing this may be guessing at the unfamiliar halogen.
